body_markdown:
With[winter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/6-simple-winter-projects-for-every-vintage-car/) just around the corner, and the particular driving challenges it tends to bring, this week we’re thinking about the best car for such thankless mobility. The cheap, capable machines ideally suited for happily trudging through grimy snow and killer salt to deliver us safely to our destinations, only to be parked come springtime in favor of the “driving season” favorites we tend to dote on. One of us may have cheated/interpreted the mission more creatively, but give our picks a look and then let us know in the comments what your preferred[winter chariot](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/driving-toward-winter/) happens to be.


## WRX for Me


Flickr/Phil


Had this question been asked a week ago, I’d have said a Volvo wagon with snow tires. I’ve made it through two decades of Ohio winters without all-wheel drive, often with open-differential cars, and never had a problem because I had the right rubber.


But then I drove a first-gen Subaru WRX for the first time last Friday. What a hoot. Do you need all-wheel drive? No. But is a good system—like the Subaru’s—a lot of fun on slick surfaces? Heck yeah it is. I’d go with a Bugeye /Blobeye/Hawkeye-era car (2002–07), probably in wagon form so I could haul stuff. — *Eddy Eckart*


## A Bulletproof EA82


Wikimedia Commons/order_242


My first, and best, winter beater was indeed a Subaru wagon—a 1987 GL with front-wheel drive that turned into all-wheel-drive at the touch of a button on the gear shift lever. Bonus points: heater and A/C worked. I drove it from Texas north to Michigan to take a job there, and I wasn’t expecting to use the AWD until long after I arrived. But an unseasonable winter storm hit Nashville right before I was about to pass through, and I couldn’t have been happier with how well the $2000 Subie performed then and over the next few years. It was a rust-free car when I bought it, and was still rust-free when I sold it, which I thought was a miracle, considering where it had been…. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## Fiesta Time


Sandon Voelker


Having enjoyed trucks as winter drivers for a number of years, I’ve seen the light—or at least how well the roads are cleared up here in the great white north—and am finally willing to forgo four-wheel motivation for the ease of parking and storage in my already cramped driveway (the garage has been full for years at this point).


So I’m going with a Ford Fiesta ST with a good set of winter tires. Multiple people around me have owned one of these hot hatches, and there aren’t many bad stories floating around. There’s enough space for parts-store runs and far better fuel economy than anything else in my fleet. Who knows, it might even be the first car I’ve owned that my wife wouldn’t hate to be seen in. Not crossing my fingers. — *Kyle Smith*


## Well, If I *Have* To…


Toyota


Having managed both rear-drive during a few winters up north as well as a couple of beaters that were just a little *too* beat, I wouldn’t mind playing it safe with the next one. Just give me a 4Runner with 4WD and heated seats. It doesn’t have to be fun, or pretty, or interesting, as long as it starts and moves when the going gets cold. My Texan blood is too thin to be out in the snow tinkering and digging. — *Andrew Newton*


## A Frazzled Fozzie


Wikimedia Commons/Rudolf Stricker


I’d love to throw down the gauntlet and pick a car that’s a downright act of defiance to the weather—A Miata on snow tires! A 2WD Silverado piled with sandbags!—but my recent promotion to fatherhood has really drawn into focus what actually matters.


For that reason, I’m also going to join the Subaru bandwagon. My pick would be a ratty Forester with the quintessential rust over the rear wheels, and maybe a slight crack in the front bumper cover. If I’m being optimistic, I’ll find one with a manual transmission. I don’t really care about the power—safe, effective winter driving is rarely about maximizing grunt—so a base 2.5-liter boxer four is fine.


Maybe I’d score some oversize all-seasons or winters on Facebook Marketplace and give it a slight hoist. Oh, and this would absolutely have heated seats. Older Subaru heated seats are the best in the business; they’d scald your keister if you weren’t careful. — *Nathan Petroelje*


## A Jeep That Can’t Be Bothered


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Angeleno reporting in. I’ve driven in snow before; don’t much care for it. My daily driver is an XJ Cherokee, and I’m sure plenty of those cheap Jeeps rusted away and became one with the Earth by serving as winter beaters, so I’m doing my part by keeping mine away from snow and salt. I think the proper winter beater is the one you run on summer tires, because it never even dips into the 30s. — *Brandan Gillogly*


## My Montero, Thanks


[Bryan Gerould](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bryan-gerould/)


Top-tier winter beaters are proven steeds. When my colleague made a tough call to sell his ’98 Montero for family-friendly wheels, I was happy to take it on for seasons like these. Heated seats, hot air, and a transfer case that gives you license to procrastinate plowing out a driveway for days at a time are what make winters more enjoyable behind the wheel. I proudly wore Fluid Film as my new cologne one weekend this fall, as I’d like this “beater” to keep on keepin’ on for many more seasons. — *Bryan Gerould*


## Not Really What We Had in Mind


RM Sotheby's


Subaru is the obvious answer if you live anywhere snow falls, but as this is an exercise in make-believe, I’m going all in and escaping the weather completely. So how about this: I spend my winters working remotely in, oh… the lovely Caribbean island of Saint Lucia, where the average winter temperature is 84 degrees. All-wheel drive and heated seats are less than useless here, of course, but do you know what’s not useless in Saint Lucia? Open-air access 24/7. Fiat Jollys are a little out of my winter-beater budget, but I’d happily cruise the Soufrière-Vieux Fort Highway that loops the island in an Austin Mini Moke, the sun on my face and a virgin daiquiri in hand, smiling as I think about my colleagues scraping their stupid windshields just to go to the grocery store. See you in the spring, suckers! — *Stefan Lombard*
